rv.q: Barron's thoughtful ambivalence cuts through the occasional mess.
And yet that’s exactly what “Shhhh” manages to do.
Yet despite this busy-bee fussiness, Intimate Apparel lets us come close to its characters, close enough to see the details — the loose button, the hesitant touch — that turn and shape the story.
Clare Barron's entire play is an exorcism of sorts.
"Shhhh" is, by turns, funny and creepy, and to amplify her extraordinary derring-do, Barron also directs and plays Shareen, one of the two lead roles.
Shhhh is raw and ambitious, and because of Barron's threefold duties as writer, director, and performer, the play is steeped in her singularly brazen voice.
The play wanders through the panoply of sexual neuroses, practices, traumas, and preferences it engages without a steady enough roadmap.
I’d like to support a playwright of such obvious talent, even when the play is as disjointed as this one, and the shocks in it so often feel gratuitous.
I’m ready to proclaim myself a fan.
At the end of the day, Shhh is a tease.

cn.t: Clare Barron's intimate, explicit meditation on consent and trauma raises ambitious themes but struggles to fully develop them. Critics praise the immersive staging while noting the fragmented structure leaves ideas underexplored.
